papers.title: EXPRESS: The Double-Edged Offline Touchpoint: How Self-Pickup Stations Reshape Pure-Play E-Commerce Transactions
papers.authors: Jingcun Cao, Zhiqi Li, Chenxi Liao, Ying Xie
papers.abstract: Click-and-collect services through self-pickup stations have gained popularity as an alternative to traditional home delivery in e-commerce. This fulfillment option can increase customer purchases by enhancing post-purchase convenience and reducing transaction costs. However, increased hassle costs for customers and exposure to offline competition make the net impact uncertain. This study utilizes a Synthetic Difference-in-Differences (SDID) approach to analyze individual-level transaction data from an online shopping platform in Asia. Self-pickup station openings are found to have a positive net effect on customer spending and shopping frequency on the platform, without cannibalizing home delivery. A closer examination of customer dynamics reveals that station openings stabilize the platform’s user base by reducing customer churn and deepening engagement among existing shoppers, rather than driving new user acquisition. Furthermore, these positive effects are moderated by: station accessibility, level of nearby offline competition, and product attributes. Specifically, this paper provides the first empirical evidence that the positive effect of pickup stations can be reduced, if platforms locate them close to major offline retail alternatives. These findings provide important implications for e-commerce platforms regarding self-pickup station benefits, product suitability, and location strategy to reduce the risk of customer loss to offline retailers.

papers.title: Brand-Neutral Content Marketing and Endogenous Search Prominence
papers.abstract: Brand-neutral content marketing attracts consumers by addressing category-level needs without directly promoting the brand. Although this may position a firm as consumers’ first point of inquiry, it leaves consumers only partially informed about brand fit. Rivals can exploit this gap by providing brand-specific information. Using a game-theoretic framework, we examine when content marketing generates endogenous search prominence and how the resulting search dynamics shape competitive communication strategies. We show that content marketing can provide a counterintuitive competitive edge: by shaping the information structure of consumer search, it influences rival pricing incentives, giving rise to asymmetric communication equilibria sustained by an information–exploitation tradeoff that governs profit allocation between the prominent gatekeeper and the non-prominent follower. When prices cannot be credibly committed, exploitation permanently dominates and content marketing becomes the unique equilibrium strategy. Brand strength and appeal breadth further determine which firm adopts content marketing.

papers.title: Rating an Experience Makes People Notice How It Is Changing: Consequences for Hedonic Adaptation and Consumer Enjoyment
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  Repeated measurement is common in both marketing research and practice. For example, experimenters often ask participants to evaluate multiple similar products, and service providers regularly check in to see how customers are doing. Such practices rest on the assumption that collecting more data simply reveals consumers’ experiences and preferences as they evolve over time. We find that repeated measurement also shapes them. Specifically, repeatedly probing consumers about an experience draws attention to how it is changing, prompting consumers to notice incremental differences more than if they were probed less or simply left alone. This process has important consequences for hedonic adaptation and enjoyment. In contexts of negative change, repeated ratings exacerbate adaptation by making incremental declines more salient, accelerating boredom and disengagement. In contexts of positive change, repeated ratings enhance experiences by making incremental improvements more salient. Sixteen studies (N = 16,311), spanning diverse hedonic stimuli (including games, foods, songs, videos, and artwork) and methodological approaches (including mediation and moderation), highlight this core idea that change is amplified when ratings draw attention to it. We discuss how repeated measurement may thereby distort understandings of hedonic decline and consumer preferences, and how to harness these insights to promote longer-lasting consumer enjoyment.
